title: The Wise Washerman's Silent Donkey
summary: A quarrelsome neighbor screams insults at an old washerman. The washerman remains silent, using his donkey to illustrate the beauty of composure.
full_text:
In the riverside quarter of Agra lived a gentle, elderly washerman named Shankar, whose calm temperament was respected by all. However, his neighbor, an aggressive and foul-mouthed blacksmith named Mangal, constantly picked quarrels, shouting vile insults and cursing at the old man over everyday trifles.

Throughout every verbal attack, Shankar never raised his voice, never frowned, and never uttered a single word in reply; he merely washed his clothes and smiled.

One morning, after the blacksmith had spent twenty minutes screaming curses at Shankar's fence, Emperor Akbar and Birbal happened to pass by on their morning ride.

Akbar stopped his horse and asked: 'Shankar, why do you stand there quietly while that scoundrel heaps filthy insults upon your head? Are you a coward, or do you have no tongue to defend your honor?'

Shankar bowed with folded hands: 'Sire, allow me to ask my donkey.'

The washerman turned to his grey donkey tied to the acacia tree. The blacksmith was still screaming. The donkey chewed its hay peacefully, flicked an occasional fly with its ear, and never once looked at the screaming man.

Shankar said to the Emperor:

'Your Majesty, look at my humble donkey. Even this simple beast understands that when a wild dog barks at the fence, the donkey does not drop its hay to bark back!

'If someone offers you an ugly, filthy package wrapped in dirty rags, and you refuse to stretch out your hands to accept it—to whom does the package still belong?'

Akbar replied: 'It still belongs to the person who brought it.'

'Exactly so, Sire!' Shankar smiled. 'My neighbor brings a package of filthy anger and hatred every morning. I simply refuse to accept it.

'Since I do not receive it, his anger remains entirely his own burden, poisoning his own blood and giving him high fever, while my soul remains peaceful and clean as river water!'

Akbar was captivated by the old washerman's profound philosophy. He ordered the abusive blacksmith fined for disturbing the peace, and commended Shankar and Birbal, remarking that composure is the highest armor of the wise.
moral: Silence is often the most profound rebuke to foolishness; do not waste words on the obstinate.
